entries.a5b6326e3c5ebcee94cf7e42ad0b99ba407e9c2f: <div sID="gen10716" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="22" osisID="Ps.22" sID="Ps.22"/> <div eID="gen10716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10717" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10718" type="x-p"/> The Spirit of Christ, which was in the prophets, testifies in this psalm, as clearly and fully as any where in all the Old Testament, "the sufferings of Christ and the glory that should follow" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 11</reference>); of him, no doubt, David here speaks, and not of himself, or any other man. Much of it is expressly applied to Christ in the New Testament, all of it may be applied to him, and some of it must be understood of him only. The providences of God concerning David were so very extraordinary that we may suppose there were some wise and good men who then could not but look upon him as a figure of him that was to come. But the composition of his psalms especially, in which he found himself wonderfully carried out by the spirit of prophecy far beyond his own thought and intention, was (we may suppose) an abundant satisfaction to himself that he was not only a father of the Messiah, but a figure of him. In this psalm he speaks, I. Of the humiliation of Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.1-Ps.22.21">ver. 1-21</reference>), where David, as a type of Christ, complains of the very calamitous condition he was in upon many accounts. 1. He complains, and mixes comforts with his complaints; he complains (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.1-Ps.22.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>), but comforts himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.3-Ps.22.5">ver. 3-5</reference>), complains again (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.6-Ps.22.8">ver. 6-8</reference>), but comforts himself again, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.9-Ps.22.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>. 2. He complains, and mixes prayers with his complaints; he complains of the power and rage of his enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.12-Ps.22.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.18">18</reference>), of his own bodily weakness and decay (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.14-Ps.22.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.17">17</reference>); but prays that God would not be far from him (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.11">ver. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.19">19</reference>), that he would save and deliver him, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.19-Ps.22.21">ver. 19-21</reference>. II. Of the exaltation of Christ, that his undertaking should be for the glory of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.22-Ps.22.25">ver. 22-25</reference>), for the salvation and joy of his people (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.26-Ps.22.29">ver. 26-29</reference>), and for the perpetuating of his own kingdom, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.30-Ps.22.31">ver. 30, 31</reference>. In singing this psalm we must keep our thoughts fixed upon Christ, and be so affected with his sufferings as to experience the fellowship of them, and so affected with his grace as to experience the power and influence of it.
entries.f1863c731f43a3ab39dc2a2243229322c8f1aaec: <div eID="gen10718" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10717" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Sorrowful Complaints.</title> <div sID="gen10719" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? <hi type="italic">why art thou so</hi> far from helping me, <hi type="italic">and from</hi> the words of my roaring? <hi type="super">2</hi> O my God, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent. 3 But thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> holy, <hi type="italic">O thou</hi> that inhabitest the praises of Israel. <hi type="super">4</hi> Our fathers trusted in thee: they trusted, and thou didst deliver them. <hi type="super">5</hi> They cried unto thee, and were delivered: they trusted in thee, and were not confounded. <hi type="super">6</hi> But I <hi type="italic">am</hi> a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people. <hi type="super">7</hi> All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> <hi type="super">8</hi> He trusted on the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">that</hi> he would deliver him: let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him. <hi type="super">9</hi> But thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> he that took me out of the womb: thou didst make me hope <hi type="italic">when I was</hi> upon my mother's breasts. <hi type="super">10</hi> I was cast upon thee from the womb: thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my God from my mother's belly. <div eID="gen10719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10720" type="x-p"/> Some think they find Christ in the title of this psalm, upon <hi type="italic">Aijeleth Shahar</hi>—<hi type="italic">The hind of the morning.</hi> Christ is as the swift hind upon the mountains of spices (<reference osisRef="Song.8.14">Cant. viii. 14</reference>), as the loving hind and the pleasant roe, to all believers (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.19">Prov. v. 19</reference>); he giveth goodly words like Naphtali, who is compared to a <hi type="italic">hind let loose,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.49.21">Gen. xlix. 21</reference>. He is the hind of the morning, marked out by the counsels of God from eternity, to be run down by those dogs that compassed him, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">v. 16</reference>. But others think it denotes only the tune to which the psalm was set. In these verses we have, <div eID="gen10720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10721" type="x-p"/> I. A sad complaint of God's withdrawings, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.1-Ps.22.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen10721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10722" type="x-p"/> 1. This may be applied to David, or any other child of God, in the want of the tokens of his favour, pressed with the burden of his displeasure, roaring under it, as one overwhelmed with grief and terror, crying earnestly for relief, and, in this case, apprehending himself forsaken of God, unhelped, unheard, yet calling him, again and again, "<hi type="italic">My God,</hi>" and continuing to cry day and night to him and earnestly desiring his gracious returns. Note, (1.) Spiritual desertions are the saints' sorest afflictions; when their evidences are clouded, divine consolations suspended, their communion with God interrupted, and the terrors of God set in array against them, how sad are their spirits, and how sapless all their comforts! (2.) Even their complaint of these burdens is a good sign of spiritual life and spiritual senses exercised. To cry out, "My God, why am I sick? Why am I poor?" would give cause to suspect discontent and worldliness. But, <hi type="italic">Why has though forsaken me?</hi> is the language of a heart binding up its happiness in God's favour. (3.) When we are lamenting God's withdrawings, yet still we must call him our God, and continue to call upon him as ours. When we want the faith of assurance we must live by a faith of adherence. "However it be, yet God is good, and he is mine; <hi type="italic">though he slay me, yet I trust in him;</hi> though he do not answer me immediately, I will continue praying and waiting; though he be silent, I will not be silent." <div eID="gen10722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10723" type="x-p"/> 2. But it must be applied to Christ: for, in the first words of this complaint, he poured out his soul before God when he was upon the cross (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.46">Matt. xxvii. 46</reference>); probably he proceeded to the following words, and, some think, repeated the whole psalm, if not aloud (because they cavilled at the first words), yet to himself. Note, (1.) Christ, in his sufferings, cried earnestly to his Father for his favour and presence with him. He cried <hi type="italic">in the day-time,</hi> upon the cross, <hi type="italic">and in the night-season,</hi> when he was in agony in the garden. <hi type="italic">He offered up strong crying and tears to him that was able to save him,</hi> and with some fear too, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>. (2.) Yet God forsook him, was far from helping him, and did not hear him, and it was this that he complained of more than all his sufferings. God delivered him into the hands of his enemies; it was by his determinate counsel that he was crucified and slain, and he did not give in sensible comforts. But, Christ having made himself sin for us, in conformity thereunto the Father laid him under the present impressions of his wrath and displeasure against sin. <hi type="italic">It pleased the Lord to bruise him and put him to grief,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Isa. liii. 10</reference>. But even then he kept fast hold of his relation to his Father as his God, by whom he was now employed, whom he was now serving, and with whom he should shortly be glorified. <div eID="gen10723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10724" type="x-p"/> II. Encouragement taken, in reference hereunto, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.3-Ps.22.5">v. 3-5</reference>. Though God did not hear him, did not help him, yet, 1. He will think well of God: "<hi type="italic">But thou art holy,</hi> not unjust, untrue, nor unkind, in any of thy dispensations. Though thou dost not immediately come in to the relief of thy afflicted people, yet though lovest them, art true to thy covenant with them, and dost not countenance the iniquity of their persecutors, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.13">Hab. i. 13</reference>. And, as thou art infinitely pure and upright thyself, so thou delightest in the services of thy upright people: <hi type="italic">Thou inhabitest the praises of Israel;</hi> thou art pleased to manifest thy glory, and grace, and special presence with thy people, in the sanctuary, where they attend thee with their praises. There thou art always ready to receive their homage, and of the tabernacle of meeting thou hast said, <hi type="italic">This is my rest for ever.</hi>" This bespeaks God's wonderful condescension to his faithful worshippers—(that, though he is attended with the praises of angels, yet he is pleased to inhabit the praises of Israel), and it may comfort us in all our complaints—that, though God seem, for a while, to turn a deaf ear to them, yet he is so well pleased with his people's praises that he will, in due time, give them cause to change their note: <hi type="italic">Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him.</hi> Our Lord Jesus, in his sufferings, had an eye to the holiness of God, to preserve and advance the honour of that, and of his grace in inhabiting the praises of Israel notwithstanding the iniquities of their holy things. 2. He will take comfort from the experiences which the saints in former ages had of the benefit of faith and prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.4-Ps.22.5">v. 4, 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Our fathers trusted in thee, cried unto thee, and thou didst deliver them;</hi> therefore thou wilt, in due time, deliver me, for never any that hoped in thee were made ashamed of their hope, never any that sought thee sought thee in vain. And thou art still the same in thyself and the same to thy people that ever thou wast. They were our fathers, and thy people are <hi type="italic">beloved for the fathers' sake,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Rom.11.28">Rom. xi. 28</reference>. The entail of the covenant is designed for the support of the seed of the faithful. He that was our fathers' God must be ours, and will therefore be ours. Our Lord Jesus, in his sufferings, supported himself with this—that all the fathers who were types of him in his sufferings, Noah, Joseph, David, Jonah, and others, were in due time delivered and were types of his exaltation too; therefore he knew that <hi type="italic">he also should not be confounded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.50.7">Isa. l. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen10724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10725" type="x-p"/> III. The complaint renewed of another grievance, and that is the contempt and reproach of men. This complaint is by no means so bitter as that before of God's withdrawings; but, as that touches a gracious soul, so this a generous soul, in a very tender part, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.6-Ps.22.8">v. 6-8</reference>. Our fathers were honoured, the patriarchs in their day, first or last, appeared great in the eye of the world, Abraham, Moses, David; but Christ is <hi type="italic">a worm, and no man.</hi> It was great condescension that he became man, a step downwards, which is, and will be, the wonder of angels; yet, as if it were too much, too great, to be a man, he becomes a worm, and no man. He was <hi type="italic">Adam—a mean man,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Enosh—a man of sorrows,</hi> but <hi type="italic">lo Ish—not a considerable man:</hi> for he took upon him the form of a servant, and <hi type="italic">his visage was marred more than any man's,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.52.14">Isa. lii. 14</reference>. Man, at the best, is a worm; but he became <hi type="italic">a worm, and no man.</hi> If he had not made himself a worm, he could not have been trampled upon as he was. The word signifies such a worm as was used in dyeing scarlet or purple, whence some make it an allusion to his bloody sufferings. See what abuses were put upon him. 1. He was reproached as a bad man, as a blasphemer, a sabbath-breaker, a wine-bibber, a false prophet, an enemy to Cæsar, a confederate with the prince of the devils. 2. He was despised of the people as a mean contemptible man, not worth taking notice of, his country in no repute, his relations poor mechanics, his followers none of the rulers, or the Pharisees, but the mob. 3. He was ridiculed as a foolish man, and one that not only deceived others, but himself too. Those that saw him hanging on the cross laughed him to scorn. So far were they from pitying him, or concerning themselves for him, that they added to his afflictions, with all the gestures and expressions of insolence upbraiding him with his fall. They make mouths at him, make merry over him, and make a jest of his sufferings: <hi type="italic">They shoot out the lip, they shake their head,</hi> saying, This was he that said <hi type="italic">he trusted God would deliver him; now let him deliver him.</hi> David was sometimes taunted for his confidence in God; but in the sufferings of Christ this was literally and exactly fulfilled. Those very gestures were used by those that reviled him (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.39">Matt. xxvii. 39</reference>); they wagged their heads, nay, and so far did their malice make them forget themselves that they used the very words (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.43">v. 43</reference>), <hi type="italic">He trusted in God; let him deliver him.</hi> Our Lord Jesus, having undertaken to satisfy for the dishonour we had done to God by our sins, did it by submitting to the lowest possible instance of ignominy and disgrace. <div eID="gen10725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10726" type="x-p"/> IV. Encouragement taken as to this also (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.9-Ps.22.10">v. 9, 10</reference>): Men despise me, <hi type="italic">but thou art he that took me out of the womb.</hi> David and other good men have often, for direction to us, encouraged themselves with this, that God was not only the <hi type="italic">God of their fathers,</hi> as before (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.4">v. 4</reference>), but the God of their infancy, who began by times to take care of them, as soon as they had a being, and therefore, they hope, will never cast them off. He that did so well for us in that helpless useless state will not leave us when he has reared us and nursed us up into some capacity of serving him. See the early instances of God's providential care for us, 1. In the birth: <hi type="italic">He took us also out of the womb,</hi> else we had died there, or been stifled in the birth. Every man's particular time begins with this pregnant proof of God's providence, as time, in general, began with the creation, that pregnant proof of his being. 2. At the breast: "<hi type="italic">Then didst thou make me hope;</hi>" that is, "thou didst that for me, in providing sustenance for me and protecting me from the dangers to which I was exposed, which encourages me to hope in thee all my days." The blessings of the breasts, as they crown the blessings of the womb, so they are earnests of the blessings of our whole lives; surely he that fed us then will never starve us, <reference osisRef="Job.3.12">Job iii. 12</reference>. 3. In our early dedication to him: <hi type="italic">I was cast upon thee from the womb,</hi> which perhaps refers to his circumcision on the eighth day; he was then by his parents committed and given up to God as his God in covenant; for circumcision was a seal of the covenant; and this encouraged him to trust in God. Those have reason to think themselves safe who were so soon, so solemnly, <hi type="italic">gathered under the wings of the divine majesty.</hi> 4. In the experience we have had of God's goodness to us all along ever since, drawn out in a constant uninterrupted series of preservations and supplies: <hi type="italic">Thou art my God,</hi> providing me and watching over me for good, <hi type="italic">from my mother's belly,</hi> that is, from my coming into the world unto this day. And if, as soon as we became capable of exercising reason, we put our confidence in God and committed ourselves and our way to him, we need not doubt but he will always remember the <hi type="italic">kindness of our youth and the love of our espousals,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jer. ii. 2</reference>. This is applicable to our Lord Jesus, over whose incarnation and birth the divine Providence watched with a peculiar care, when he was born in a stable, laid in a manger, and immediately exposed to the malice of Herod, and forced to flee into Egypt. <hi type="italic">When he was a child God loved him and called him thence</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.1">Hos. xi. 1</reference>), and the remembrance of this comforted him in his sufferings. Men reproached him, and discouraged his confidence in God; but God had honoured him and encouraged his confidence in him.
entries.2220baf8ecd928c9323ee9796e6229047b307e23: <div eID="gen10726" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sufferings of the Messiah; The Messiah Supported in His Sufferings.</title> <div sID="gen10727" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Be not far from me; for trouble <hi type="italic">is</hi> near; for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none to help. <hi type="super">12</hi> Many bulls have compassed me: strong <hi type="italic">bulls</hi> of Bashan have beset me round. 13 They gaped upon me <hi type="italic">with</hi> their mouths, <hi type="italic">as</hi> a ravening and a roaring lion. <hi type="super">14</hi> I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint: my heart is like wax; it is melted in the midst of my bowels. <hi type="super">15</hi> My strength is dried up like a potsherd; and my tongue cleaveth to my jaws; and thou hast brought me into the dust of death. <hi type="super">16</hi> For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet. <hi type="super">17</hi> I may tell all my bones: they look <hi type="italic">and</hi> stare upon me. <hi type="super">18</hi> They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture. <hi type="super">19</hi> But be not thou far from me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> : O my strength, haste thee to help me. <hi type="super">20</hi> Deliver my soul from the sword; my darling from the power of the dog. <hi type="super">21</hi> Save me from the lion's mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns. <div eID="gen10727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10728" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have Christ suffering and Christ praying, by which we are directed to look for crosses and to look up to God under them. <div eID="gen10728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10729" type="x-p"/> I. Here is Christ suffering. David indeed was often in trouble, and beset with enemies; but many of the particulars here specified are such as were never true of David, and therefore must be appropriated to Christ in the depth of his humiliation. <div eID="gen10729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10730" type="x-p"/> 1. He is here deserted by his friends: <hi type="italic">Trouble</hi> and distress are <hi type="italic">near,</hi> and <hi type="italic">there is none to help,</hi> none to uphold, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.11">v. 11</reference>. He trod the wine-press alone; for all his disciples forsook him and fled. It is God's honour to help when all other helps and succours fail. <div eID="gen10730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10731" type="x-p"/> 2. He is here insulted and surrounded by his enemies, such as were of a higher rank, who for their strength and fury, are compared to bulls, <hi type="italic">strong bulls of Bashan</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.12">v. 12</reference>), fat and fed to the full, haughty and sour; such were the chief priests and elders that persecuted Christ; and others of a lower rank, who are compared to dogs (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">v. 16</reference>), filthy and greedy, and unwearied in running him down. There was an assembly of the wicked plotting against him (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">v. 16</reference>); for the chief priests sat in council, to consult of ways and means to take Christ. These enemies were numerous and unanimous: "Many, and those of different and clashing interests among themselves, as Herod and Pilate, have agreed to compass me. They have carried their plot far, and seem to have gained their point, for they have <hi type="italic">beset me round,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.22.12">v. 12</reference>. They have enclosed me, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">v. 16</reference>. They are formidable and threatening (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">They gaped upon me with their mouths,</hi> to show me that they would swallow me up; and this with as much strength and fierceness as a roaring ravening lion leaps upon his prey." <div eID="gen10731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10732" type="x-p"/> 3. He is here crucified. The very manner of his death is described, though never in use among the Jews: <hi type="italic">They pierced my hands and my feet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">v. 16</reference>), which were nailed to the accursed tree, and the whole body left so to hang, the effect of which must needs be the most exquisite pain and torture. There is no one passage in all the Old Testament which the Jews have so industriously corrupted as this, because it is such an eminent prediction of the death of Christ and was so exactly fulfilled. <div eID="gen10732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10733" type="x-p"/> 4. He is here dying (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.14-Ps.22.15">v. 14, 15</reference>), dying in pain and anguish, because he was to satisfy for sin, which brought in pain, and for which we must otherwise have lain in everlasting anguish. Here is, (1.) The dissolution of the whole frame of his body: <hi type="italic">I am poured out like water,</hi> weak as water, and yielding to the power of death, emptying himself of all the supports of his human nature. (2.) The dislocation of his bones. Care was taken that not one of them should be broken (<reference osisRef="John.19.36">John xix. 36</reference>), but they were all out of joint by the violent stretching of his body upon the cross as upon a rack. Or it may denote the fear that seized him in his agony in the garden, when he began to be sore amazed, the effect of which perhaps was (as sometimes it has been of great fear, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.6">Dan. v. 6</reference>), that the <hi type="italic">joints of his loins were loosed and his knees smote one against another.</hi> His bones were put out of joint that he might put the whole creation into joint again, which sin had put out of joint, and might make our broken bones to rejoice. (3.) The colliquation of his spirits: <hi type="italic">My heart is like wax,</hi> melted to receive the impressions of God's wrath against the sins he undertook to satisfy for, melting away like the vitals of a dying man; and, as this satisfied for the hardness of our hearts, so the consideration of it should help to soften them. When Job speaks of his inward trouble he says, <hi type="italic">The Almighty makes my heart soft,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.23.16">Job xxiii. 16</reference>, and see <reference osisRef="Ps.58.2">Ps. lviii. 2</reference>. (4.) The failing of his natural force: <hi type="italic">My strength is dried up;</hi> so that he became parched and brittle like a potsherd, the radical moisture being wasted by the fire of divine wrath preying upon his spirits. Who then can stand before God's anger? Or who knows the power of it? <hi type="italic">If this was done in the green tree, what shall be done in the dry?</hi> (5.) The clamminess of his mouth, a usual symptom of approaching death: <hi type="italic">My tongue cleaveth to my jaws;</hi> this was fulfilled both in his thirst upon the cross (<reference osisRef="John.19.28">John xix. 28</reference>) and in his silence under his sufferings; for, <hi type="italic">as a sheep before the shearers is dumb, so he opened not his mouth,</hi> nor objected against any thing done to him. (6.) His giving up the ghost: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast brought me to the dust of death;</hi> I am just ready to drop into the grave;" for nothing less would satisfy divine justice. The life of the sinner was forfeited, and therefore the life of the sacrifice must be the ransom for it. The sentence of death passed upon Adam was thus expressed: <hi type="italic">Unto dust thou shalt return.</hi> And therefore Christ, having an eye to that sentence in his obedience to death, here uses a similar expression: <hi type="italic">Thou hast brought me to the dust of death.</hi> <div eID="gen10733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10734" type="x-p"/> 5. He was stripped. The shame of nakedness was the immediate consequence of sin; and therefore our Lord Jesus was stripped of his clothes, when he was crucified, that he might clothe us with the robe of his righteousness, and that the shame of our nakedness might not appear. Now here we are told, (1.) How his body looked when it was thus stripped: <hi type="italic">I may tell all my bones,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.22.17">v. 17</reference>. His blessed body was lean and emaciated with labour, grief, and fasting, during the whole course of his ministry, which made him look as if he was nearly 50 years old when he was yet but 33, as we find, <reference osisRef="John.8.57">John viii. 57</reference>. His wrinkles now witnessed for him that he was far from being what was called, <hi type="italic">a gluttonous man and a wine-bibber.</hi> Or his bones might be numbered, because his body was distended upon the cross, which made it easy to count his ribs. <hi type="italic">They look and stare upon me,</hi> that is, my bones do, being distorted, and having no flesh to cover them, as Job says (<reference osisRef="Job.16.8">ch. xvi. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">My leanness, rising up in me, beareth witness to my face.</hi> Or "the standers by, the passers by, are amazed to see my bones start out thus; and, instead of pitying me, are pleased even with such a rueful spectacle." (2.) What they did with his clothes, which they took from him (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">They parted my garments among them,</hi> to every soldier a part, and <hi type="italic">upon my vesture,</hi> the seamless coat, <hi type="italic">do they cast lots.</hi> This very circumstance was exactly fulfilled, <reference osisRef="John.19.23-John.19.24">John xix. 23, 24</reference>. And though it was no great instance of Christ's suffering, yet it is a great instance of the fulfilling of the scripture in him. <hi type="italic">Thus it was written, and</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">thus it behoved Christ to suffer.</hi> Let this therefore confirm our faith in him as the true Messiah, and inflame our love to him as the best of friends, who loved us and suffered all this for us. <div eID="gen10734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10735" type="x-p"/> II. Here is Christ praying, and with that supporting himself under the burden of his sufferings. Christ, in his agony, prayed earnestly, prayed that the cup might pass from him. When the prince of this world with his terrors set upon him, <hi type="italic">gaped upon him as a roaring lion,</hi> he fell upon the ground and prayed. And of that David's praying here was a type. He calls God his <hi type="italic">strength,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.22.19">v. 19</reference>. When we cannot rejoice in God as our song, yet let us stay ourselves upon him as out strength, and take the comfort of spiritual supports when we cannot come at spiritual delights. He prays, 1. That God would be with him, and not set himself at a distance from him: <hi type="italic">Be not thou far from me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.11">v. 11</reference>), and again, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.19">v. 19</reference>. "Whoever stands aloof from my sore, Lord, do not thou." The nearness of trouble should quicken us to draw near to God and then we may hope that he will draw near to us. 2. That he would help him and make haste to help him, help him to bear up under his troubles, that he might not fail nor be discouraged, that he might neither shrink from his undertaking nor sink under it. And the Father <hi type="italic">heard him in that he feared</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>) and enabled him to go through with his work. 3. That he would deliver him and save him, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.20-Ps.22.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. (1.) Observe what the jewel is which he is in care for, "The safety of my soul, my darling; let that be redeemed from the power of the grave, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.15">Ps. xlix. 15</reference>. Father, into thy hands I commit that, to be conveyed safely to paradise." The psalmist here calls his soul his <hi type="italic">darling,</hi> his <hi type="italic">only one</hi> (so the word is): "<hi type="italic">My soul</hi> is <hi type="italic">my only one.</hi> I have but one soul to take care of, and therefore the greater is my shame if I neglect it and the greater will the loss be if I let it perish. Being my only one, it ought to be my darling, for the eternal welfare of which I ought to be deeply concerned. I do not use my soul as my darling, unless I take care to preserve it from every thing that would hurt it and to provide all necessaries for it, and be entirely tender of its welfare." (2.) Observe what the danger is from which he prays to be delivered, <hi type="italic">from the sword,</hi> the flaming sword of divine wrath, which turns every way. This he dreaded more than any thing, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.24">Gen. iii. 24</reference>. God's anger was the wormwood and the gall in the bitter cup that was put into his hands. "O deliver my soul from that. Lord, though I lose my life, let me not lose thy love. Save me from <hi type="italic">the power of the dog,</hi> and <hi type="italic">from the lion's mouth.</hi>" This seems to be meant of Satan, that old enemy who bruised the heel of the seed of the woman, the prince of this world, with whom he was to engage in close combat and whom he saw coming, <reference osisRef="John.14.30">John xiv. 30</reference>. "Lord, save me from being overpowered by his terrors." He pleads, "Thou hast formerly <hi type="italic">heard me from the horns of the unicorn,</hi>" that is, "saved me from him in answer to my prayer." This may refer to the victory Christ had obtained over Satan and his temptations (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.1-Matt.4.11">Matt. iv.</reference>), when the devil left him for a season (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.13">Luke iv. 13</reference>), but now returned in another manner to attack him with his terrors. "Lord, thou gavest me the victory then, give it me now, that I may spoil principalities and powers, and <hi type="italic">cast out the prince of this world.</hi>" Has God delivered us <hi type="italic">from the horns of the unicorn,</hi> that we be not tossed? Let that encourage us to hope that we shall be delivered from the lion's mouth, that we be not torn. He that has delivered doth and will deliver. This prayer of Christ, no doubt, was answered, for the Father heard him always. And, though he did not deliver him from death, yet he suffered him not to see corruption, but, the third day, raised him out of the dust of death, which was a greater instance of God's favour to him than if he had helped him down from the cross; for that would have hindered his undertaking, whereas his resurrection crowned it. <div eID="gen10735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10736" type="x-p"/> In singing this we should meditate on the sufferings and resurrection of Christ till we experience in our own souls the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings.
entries.21c3c1c04d27b8e633d82e9ec07b1c11ee656ad9: <div eID="gen10736" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Messiah's Triumphs; Extension and Perpetuity of the Church.</title> <div sID="gen10737" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee. <hi type="super">23</hi> Ye that fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , praise him; all ye the seed of Jacob, glorify him; and fear him, all ye the seed of Israel. <hi type="super">24</hi> For he hath not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted; neither hath he hid his face from him; but when he cried unto him, he heard. <hi type="super">25</hi> My praise <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> of thee in the great congregation: I will pay my vows before them that fear him. <hi type="super">26</hi> The meek shall eat and be satisfied: they shall praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that seek him: your heart shall live for ever. <hi type="super">27</hi> All the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and all the kindreds of the nations shall worship before thee. <hi type="super">28</hi> For the kingdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's: and he <hi type="italic">is</hi> the governor among the nations. <hi type="super">29</hi> All <hi type="italic">they that be</hi> fat upon earth shall eat and worship: all they that go down to the dust shall bow before him: and none can keep alive his own soul. <hi type="super">30</hi> A seed shall serve him; it shall be accounted to the Lord for a generation. <hi type="super">31</hi> They shall come, and shall declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done <hi type="italic">this.</hi> <div eID="gen10737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10738" type="x-p"/> The same that began the psalm complaining, who was no other than Christ in his humiliation, ends it here triumphing, and it can be no other than Christ in his exaltation. And, as the first words of the complaint were used by Christ himself upon the cross, so the first words of the triumph are expressly applied to him (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.12">Heb. ii. 12</reference>) and are made his own words: <hi type="italic">I will declare thy name unto my brethren, in the midst of the church will I sing praise unto thee.</hi> The certain prospect which Christ had of the joy set before him not only gave him a satisfactory answer to his prayers, but turned his complaints into praises; he saw of the travail of his soul, and was well satisfied, witness that triumphant word wherewith he breathed his last: <hi type="italic">It is finished.</hi> <div eID="gen10738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10739" type="x-p"/> Five things are here spoken of, the view of which were the satisfaction and triumph of Christ in his sufferings:— <div eID="gen10739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10740" type="x-p"/> I. That he should have a church in the world, and that those that were given him from eternity should, in the fulness of time, be gathered in to him. This is implied here; that he should <hi type="italic">see his seed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Isa. liii. 10</reference>. It pleased him to think, 1. That by the declaring of God's name, by the preaching of the everlasting gospel in its plainness and purity, many should be effectually called to him and to God by him. And for this end ministers should be employed to publish this doctrine to the world, and they should be much his messengers and his voice that their doing it should be accounted his doing it; their word is his, and by them he declares God's name. 2. That those who are thus called in should be brought into a very near and dear relation to him as his brethren; for he is not only not ashamed, but greatly well pleased, to call them so; not the believing Jews only, his countrymen, but those of the Gentiles also who became fellow-heirs and of the same body, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.11">Heb. ii. 11</reference>. Christ is our elder brother, who takes care of us, and makes provision for us, and expects that our desire should be towards him and that we should be willing he should rule over us. 3. That these is brethren should be incorporated into a congregation, a great congregation; such is the universal church, the whole family that is named from him, unto which all the <hi type="italic">children of God that were scattered abroad are collected,</hi> and in which they are united (<reference osisRef="John.11.52">John xi. 52</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Eph. i. 10</reference>), and that they should also be incorporated into smaller societies, members of that great body, many religious assemblies for divine worship, on which the face of Christianity should appear and in which the interests of it should be supported and advanced. 4. That these should be accounted the seed of Jacob and Israel (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.23">v. 23</reference>), that on them, though Gentiles, the blessing of Abraham might come (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.14">Gal. iii. 14</reference>), and to them might pertain the adoption, the glory, the covenant, and the service of God, as much as ever they did to <hi type="italic">Israel according to the flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Rom. ix. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.10">Heb. viii. 10</reference>. The gospel church is called <hi type="italic">the Israel of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.6.16">Gal. vi. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen10740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10741" type="x-p"/> II. That God should be greatly honoured and glorified in him by that church. His Father's glory was that which he had in his eye throughout his whole undertaking (<reference osisRef="John.17.4">John xvii. 4</reference>), particularly in his sufferings, which he entered upon with this solemn request, <hi type="italic">Father, glorify thy name,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.27-John.12.28">John xii. 27, 28</reference>. He foresees with pleasure, 1. That God would be glorified by the church that should be gathered to him, and that for this end they should be called and gathered in that they might be unto God <hi type="italic">for a name and a praise.</hi> Christ by his ministers will declare God's name to his brethren, as God's mouth to them, and then by them, as the mouth of the congregation to God, will God's name be praised. All that fear the Lord will praise him (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.23">v. 23</reference>), even every Israelite indeed. See <reference osisRef="Ps.118.2-Ps.118.4">Ps. cxviii. 2-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.135.19-Ps.135.20">cxxxv. 19, 20</reference>. The business of Christians, particularly in their solemn religious assemblies, is to praise and glorify God with a holy awe and reverence of his majesty, and therefore those that are here called upon to praise God are called upon to fear him. 2. That God would be glorified in the Redeemer and in his undertaking. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> Christ is said to <hi type="italic">praise God in the church,</hi> not only because he is the Master of the assemblies in which God is praised, and the Mediator of all the praises that are offered up to God, but because he is the matter of the church's praise. See <reference osisRef="Eph.3.21">Eph. iii. 21</reference>. All our praises must centre in the work of redemption and a great deal of reason we have to be thankful, (1.) That Jesus Christ was owned by his Father in his undertaking, notwithstanding the apprehension he was sometimes under that his Father had forsaken him. (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">For he hath not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted</hi> one (that is, of the suffering Redeemer), but has graciously accepted it as a full satisfaction for sin, and a valuable consideration on which to ground the grant of eternal life to all believers. Though it was offered for us poor sinners, he did not despise nor abhor him that offered it for our sakes; nor did he turn his face from him that offered it, as Saul was angry with his own son because he interceded for David, whom he looked upon as his enemy. But when he cried unto him, when his blood cried for peace and pardon for us, he heard him. This, as it is the matter of our rejoicing, ought to be the matter of our thanksgiving. Those who have thought their prayers slighted and unheard, if they continue to pray and wait, will find they have not sought in vain. (2.) That he himself will go on with his undertaking and complete it. Christ says, <hi type="italic">I will pay my vows,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.22.25">v. 25</reference>. Having engaged to bring many sons to glory, he will perform his engagement to the utmost, and will lose none. <div eID="gen10741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10742" type="x-p"/> III. That all humble gracious souls should have a full satisfaction and happiness in him, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.26">v. 26</reference>. It comforted the Lord Jesus in his sufferings that in and through him all true believers should have everlasting consolation. 1. The poor in spirit shall be rich in blessings, spiritual blessings; the hungry shall be filled with good things. Christ's sacrifice being accepted, the saints shall feast upon the sacrifice, as, under the law, upon the peace-offerings, and so partake of the altar: <hi type="italic">The meek shall eat and be satisfied,</hi> eat of the bread of life, feed with an appetite upon the doctrine of Christ's mediation, which is meat and drink to the soul that knows its own nature and case. Those that hunger and thirst after righteousness in Christ shall have all they can desire to satisfy them and make them easy, and shall not labour, as they have done, for that which satisfies not. 2. Those that are much in praying shall be much in thanksgiving: <hi type="italic">Those shall praise the Lord that seek him,</hi> because through Christ they are sure of finding him, in the hopes of which they have reason to praise him even while they are seeking him, and the more earnest they are in seeking him the more will their hearts be enlarged in his praises when they have found him. 3. The souls that are devoted to him shall be for ever happy with him: "<hi type="italic">Your heart shall live for ever.</hi> Yours that are meek, that are satisfied in Christ, that continue to seek God; what ever becomes of your bodies, <hi type="italic">your hearts shall live for ever;</hi> the graces and comforts you have shall be perfected in everlasting life. Christ has said, <hi type="italic">Because I live, you shall live also,</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.14.19">John xiv. 19</reference>); and therefore that life shall be as sure and as long as his." <div eID="gen10742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10743" type="x-p"/> IV. That the church of Christ, and with it the kingdom of God among men, should extend itself to all the corners of the earth and should take in all sorts of people. <div eID="gen10743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10744" type="x-p"/> 1. That it should reach far (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.27-Ps.22.28">v. 27, 28</reference>), that, whereas the Jews had long been the only professing people of God, now all the ends of the world should come into the church, and, the partition-wall being taken down, the Gentiles should be taken in. It is here prophesied, (1.) That they should be converted: They <hi type="italic">shall remember, and turn to the Lord.</hi> Note, Serious reflection is the first step, and a good step it is towards true conversion. We must consider and turn. The prodigal came first to himself, and then to his father. (2.) That then they should be admitted into communion with God and with the assemblies that serve him; <hi type="italic">They shall worship before thee,</hi> for <hi type="italic">in every place incense shall be offered to God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.1.11">Mal. i. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.23">Isa. lxvi. 23</reference>. Those that turn to God will make conscience of worshipping before him. And good reason there is why all the kindreds of nations should do homage to God, for (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.28">v. 28</reference>) <hi type="italic">the kingdom is the Lord's;</hi> his, and his only, is the universal monarchy. [1.] The kingdom of nature is the Lord Jehovah's, and his providence rules among the nations, and upon that account we are bound to worship him; so that the design of the Christian religion is to revive natural religion and its principles and laws. Christ died to bring us to God, the God that made us, from whom we had revolted, and to reduce us to our native allegiance. [2.] The kingdom of grace is the Lord Christ's, and he, as Mediator, is appointed governor among the nations, head over all things to his church. Let every tongue therefore confess that he is Lord. <div eID="gen10744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10745" type="x-p"/> 2. That it should include many of different ranks, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.29">v. 29</reference>. High and low, rich and poor, bond and free, meet in Christ. (1.) Christ shall have the homage of many of the great ones. <hi type="italic">Those that are fat upon the earth,</hi> that live in pomp and power, <hi type="italic">shall eat and worship;</hi> even those that fare deliciously, when they have eaten and are full, shall bless the Lord their God for their plenty and prosperity. (2.) The poor also shall receive his gospel: <hi type="italic">Those that go down to the dust,</hi> that sit in the dust (<reference osisRef="Ps.113.7">Ps. cxiii. 7</reference>), that can scarcely keep life and soul together, <hi type="italic">shall bow before him,</hi> before the Lord Jesus, who reckons it his honour to be the poor man's King (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.12">Ps. lxxii. 12</reference>) and whose protection does, in a special manner, draw their allegiance. Or this may be understood in general of dying men, whether poor or rich. See then what is our condition—we are going down to the dust to which we are sentenced and where shortly we must make our bed. Nor can we keep alive our own souls; we cannot secure our own natural life long, nor can we be the authors of our own spiritual and eternal life. It is therefore our great interest, as well as duty, to bow before the Lord Jesus, to give up ourselves to him to be his subjects and worshippers; for this is the only way, and it is a sure way, to secure our happiness when we go down to the dust. Seeing we cannot keep alive our own souls, it is our wisdom, by an obedient faith, to commit our souls to Jesus Christ, who is able to save them and keep them alive for ever. <div eID="gen10745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10746" type="x-p"/> V. That the church of Christ, and with it the kingdom of God among men, should continue to the end, through all the ages of time. Mankind is kept up in a succession of generations; so that there is always a generation passing away and a generation coming up. Now, as Christ shall have honour from that which is passing away and leaving the world (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.29">v. 29</reference>, <hi type="italic">those that go down to the dust shall bow before him,</hi> and it is good to die bowing before Christ; <hi type="italic">blessed are the dead who</hi> thus <hi type="italic">die in the Lord</hi>), so he shall have honour from that which is rising up, and setting out, in the world, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.30">v. 30</reference>. Observe, 1. Their application to Christ: <hi type="italic">A seed shall serve him,</hi> shall keep up the solemn worship of him and profess and practice obedience to him as their Master and Lord. Note, God will have a church in the world to the end of time; and, in order to that, there shall be a succession of professing Christians and gospel ministers from generation to generation. <hi type="italic">A seed shall serve him;</hi> there shall be a remnant, more or less, to whom shall pertain the service of God and to whom God will give grace to serve him,—perhaps not the seed of the same persons, for grace does not run in a blood (he does not say <hi type="italic">their</hi> seed, but <hi type="italic">a</hi> seed),—perhaps but few, yet enough to preserve the entail. 2. Christ's acknowledgment of them: <hi type="italic">They shall be accounted to him for a generation;</hi> he will be the same to them that he was to those who went before them; his kindness to his friends shall not die with them, but shall be drawn out to their heirs and successors, and instead of the fathers shall be the children, whom all shall acknowledge to be a <hi type="italic">seed that the Lord hath blessed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.61.9">Isa. lxi. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.23">lxv. 23</reference>. The generation of the righteous God will graciously own as his treasure, his children. 3. Their agency for him (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">they shall come,</hi> shall rise up in their day, not only to keep up the virtue of the generation that is past, and to do the work of their own generation, but to serve the honour of Christ and the welfare of souls in the generations to come; they shall transmit to them the gospel of Christ (that sacred deposit) pure and entire, even to a people that shall be born hereafter; to them they shall declare two things:—(1.) That there is an everlasting righteousness, which Jesus Christ has brought in. This righteousness of his, and not any of our own, they shall declare to be the foundation of all our hopes and the fountain of all our joys. See <reference osisRef="Rom.1.16-Rom.1.17">Rom. i. 16, 17</reference>. (2.) That the work of our redemption by Christ is the Lord's own doing (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.23">Ps. cxviii. 23</reference>) and no contrivance of ours. We must declare to our children that God has done this; it is his wisdom in a mystery; it is his arm revealed. <div eID="gen10746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10747" type="x-p"/> In singing this we must triumph in the name of Christ as above every name, must give him honour ourselves, rejoice in the honours others do him, and in the assurance we have that there shall be a people praising him on earth when we are praising him in heaven.  <chapter eID="Ps.22"/> <div eID="gen10747" type="x-p"/>

entries.4ec8ae985a2d67ca13b5729a162d880802fe2f45: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5678"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 22</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.22.1-Ps.22.31">Psa 22:1-31</reference>. The obscure words Aijeleth Shahar in this title have various explanations. Most interpreters agree in translating them by "hind of the morning." But great difference exists as to the meaning of these words. By some they are supposed (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.9.1">Psa 9:1</reference>) to be the name of the tune to which the words of the Psalm were set; by others, the name of a musical instrument. Perhaps the best view is to regard the phrase as enigmatically expressive of the subject--the sufferer being likened to a hind pursued by hunters in the early morning (literally, "the dawn of day")--or that, while hind suggests the idea of a meek, innocent sufferer, the addition of morning denotes relief obtained. The feelings of a pious sufferer in sorrow and deliverance are vividly portrayed. He earnestly pleads for divine aid on the ground of his relation to God, whose past goodness to His people encourages hope, and then on account of the imminent danger by which he is threatened. The language of complaint is turned to that of rejoicing in the assured prospect of relief from suffering and triumph over his enemies. The use of the words of the first clause of <reference osisRef="Ps.22.1">Psa 22:1</reference> by our Saviour on the cross, and the quotation of <reference osisRef="Ps.22.18">Psa 22:18</reference> by John (<reference osisRef="John.19.24">Joh 19:24</reference>), and of <reference osisRef="Ps.22.22">Psa 22:22</reference> by Paul (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.12">He 2:12</reference>), as fulfilled in His history, clearly intimate the prophetical and Messianic purport of the Psalm. The intensity of the grief, and the completeness and glory of the deliverance and triumph, alike appear to be unsuitable representations of the fortunes of any less personage. In a general and modified sense (see on <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1">Psa 16:1</reference>), the experience here detailed may be adapted to the case of all Christians suffering from spiritual foes, and delivered by divine aid, inasmuch as Christ in His human nature was their head and representative.</title> <div sID="gen8642" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5678"/>1. A summary of the complaint. Desertion by God, when overwhelmed by distress, is the climax of the sufferer's misery.<div eID="gen8642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">words of my roaring--</hi>shows that the complaint is expressed intelligently, though the term "roaring" is figurative, taken from the conduct of irrational creatures in pain. <div eID="gen8643" type="x-p"/>
entries.86f0b1821d4f6490ba9907d01d8df67d27ab17fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5679"/><div sID="gen8644" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5679"/> <hi type="bold">2. The long distress is evinced by--</hi> <div eID="gen8644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8645" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">am not silent--</hi>literally, "not silence to me," either meaning, I continually cry; or, corresponding with "thou hearest not," or answerest not, it may mean, there is no rest or quiet to me. <div eID="gen8645" type="x-p"/>
entries.f28fe56c2dfb2db43b0a66195d544cafc1570650: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5680"/><div sID="gen8646" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5680"/>3. Still he not only refrains from charging God foolishly, but evinces his confidence in God by appealing to Him.<div eID="gen8646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8647" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou art holy--</hi>or possessed of all the attributes which encourage trust, and the right object of the praises of the Church: hence the sufferer need not despair. <div eID="gen8647" type="x-p"/>
entries.42787eaa254f86af89b332b29e1d15a233eeb03b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5681"/><div sID="gen8648" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5681"/>4-5. Past experience of God's people is a ground of trust. The mention of "our fathers" does not destroy the applicability of the words as the language of our Saviour's human nature. <div eID="gen8648" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd408590f74a33176ba50407b66b5b03532851a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5682"/><div sID="gen8649" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5682"/>6. He who was despised and rejected of His own people, as a disgrace to the nation, might well use these words of deep abasement, which express not His real, but esteemed, value. <div eID="gen8649" type="x-p"/>
entries.13b0cb704f74c7463a5024fdc26c11b255c0d6c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5683"/><div sID="gen8650" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5683"/>7-8. For the Jews used one of the gestures (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.39">Mt 27:39</reference>) here mentioned, when taunting Him on the cross, and (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.43">Mt 27:43</reference>) reproached Him almost in the very, language of this passage.<div eID="gen8650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8651" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shoot out--</hi>or, "open."<div eID="gen8651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8652" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the lip--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.35.21">Psa 35:21</reference>). <div eID="gen8652" type="x-p"/>
entries.25a9145f63bfd4ba96d9fc8cd96eca970b2a16c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5685"/><div sID="gen8654" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5685"/>9-10. Though ironically spoken, the exhortation to trust was well founded on his previous experience of divine aid, the special illustration of which is drawn from the period of helpless infancy.<div eID="gen8654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8655" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">didst make me hope--</hi>literally, "made me secure." <div eID="gen8655" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b4a6fbf4ad855ec9be61f751b0c0256a950ab2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5686"/><div sID="gen8656" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5686"/>11. From this statement of reasons for the appeal, he renews it, pleading his double extremity, the nearness of trouble, and the absence of a helper. <div eID="gen8656" type="x-p"/>
entries.9e6253d7e5199dbfcb73ab87daeac3f6cc8a41d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5687"/><div sID="gen8657" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5687"/>12-13. His enemies, with the vigor of bulls and rapacity of lions, surround him, eagerly seeking his ruin. The force of both figures is greater without the use of any particle denoting comparison. <div eID="gen8657" type="x-p"/>
entries.b61b2869eed0eb57c0083420b8c6d811e0b27493: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5688"/><div sID="gen8658" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5688"/>14-15. Utter exhaustion and hopeless weakness, in these circumstances of pressing danger, are set forth by the most expressive figures; the solidity of the body is destroyed, and it becomes like water; the bones are parted; the heart, the very seat of vitality, melts like wax; all the juices of the system are dried up; the tongue can no longer perform its office, but lies parched and stiffened (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.49.4">Ge 49:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.14">2Sa 14:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.58.8">Psa 58:8</reference>). In this, God is regarded as the ultimate source, and men as the instruments. <div eID="gen8658" type="x-p"/>
entries.86bae021cf2bb350dc7d7eadcb84b6292567855d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5690"/><div sID="gen8660" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5690"/>16. Evildoers are well described as dogs, which, in the East, herding together, wild and rapacious, are justly objects of great abhorrence. The last clause has been a subject of much discussion (involving questions as to the genuineness of the Hebrew word translated "pierce)" which cannot be made intelligible to the English reader. Though not quoted in the New Testament, the remarkable aptness of the description to the facts of the Saviour's history, together with difficulties attending any other mode of explaining the clause in the Hebrew, justify an adherence to the terms of our version and their obvious meaning. <div eID="gen8660" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed5dcf4b3a12068ec31143d66835d1665bf2d82f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5691"/><div sID="gen8661" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5691"/>17. His emaciated frame, itself an item of his misery, is rendered more so as the object of delighted contemplation to his enemies. The verbs, "look" and "stare," often occur as suggestive of feelings of satisfaction (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Psa 27:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.54.7">54:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.7">118:7</reference>). <div eID="gen8661" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff268ee015ec5c07401b68a39d3c6243c7a3ba7d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5692"/><div sID="gen8662" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5692"/>18. This literally fulfilled prediction closes the sad picture of the exposed and deserted sufferer. <div eID="gen8662" type="x-p"/>
entries.509f2a62507a0e27d37b00e66b258c6072294a98: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5693"/><div sID="gen8663" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5693"/>19-20. He now turns with unabated desire and trust to God, who, in His strength and faithfulness, is contrasted with the urgent dangers described. <div eID="gen8663" type="x-p"/>
entries.7156acf3452fefe5a2c0a1ebec47f609ef5f0403: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5695"/><div sID="gen8666" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5695"/>21. Deliverance pleaded in view of former help, when in the most imminent danger, from the most powerful enemy, represented by the unicorn or wild buffalo.<div eID="gen8666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8667" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the lion's mouth--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.22.13">Psa 22:13</reference>). The lion often used as a figure representing violent enemies; the connecting of the mouth intimates their rapacity. <div eID="gen8667" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d9925be53f5f6d9ebc49e907bb5f4ca991a9d0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5696"/><div sID="gen8668" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5696"/>22-24. He declares his purpose to celebrate God's gracious dealings and publish His manifested perfections ("name," <reference osisRef="Ps.5.11">Psa 5:11</reference>), &c., and forthwith he invites the pious (those who have a reverential fear of God) to unite in special praise for a deliverance, illustrating God's kind regard for the lowly, whom men neglect [Psa 22:24]. To hide the face (or eyes) expresses a studied neglect of one's cause, and refusal of aid or sympathy (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.30.7">Psa 30:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Is 1:15</reference>). <div eID="gen8668" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4d83debdf70641be07bc9dd40eabc319e049590: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5697"/><div sID="gen8669" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5697"/><hi type="bold">25-26. My praise shall be of thee--</hi>or, perhaps better, "from thee," that is, God gives grace to praise Him. With offering praise, he further evinces his gratitude by promising the payment of his vows, in celebrating the usual festival, as provided in the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.18">De 12:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.16.11">16:11</reference>), of which the pious or humble, and they that seek the Lord (His true worshippers) shall partake abundantly, and join him in praise [Psa 22:26]. In the enthusiasm produced by his lively feelings, he addresses such in words, assuring them of God's perpetual favor [Psa 22:26]. The dying of the heart denotes death (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.37">1Sa 25:37</reference>); so its living denotes life. <div eID="gen8669" type="x-p"/>
entries.5658d1f473f400bb4892246668f4cdfb54aaa5d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5698"/><div sID="gen8670" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5698"/>27-31. His case illustrates God's righteous government. Beyond the existing time and people, others shall be brought to acknowledge and worship God; the fat ones, or the rich as well as the poor, the helpless who cannot keep themselves alive, shall together unite in celebrating God's delivering power, and transmit to unborn people the records of His grace. <div eID="gen8670" type="x-p"/>

entries.8b27a0fd4d5b0b3683c60cf5feb71a609d8f7135: <div eID="gen19183" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19184" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19185" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19185" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19184" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19186" type="x-p"/> Under great affliction and distress, the psalmist prays unto God, <reference osisRef="Psa.22.1-Psa.22.3">Psa 22:1-3</reference>; appeals to God's wonted kinkiness in behalf of his people, <reference osisRef="Psa.22.4">Psa 22:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.22.5">Psa 22:5</reference>; relates the insults that he received, <reference osisRef="Psa.22.6-Psa.22.8">Psa 22:6-8</reference>; mentions the goodness of God to him in his youth, as a reason why he should expect help now, <reference osisRef="Psa.22.9-Psa.22.11">Psa 22:9-11</reference>; details his sufferings, and the indignities offered to him, <reference osisRef="Psa.22.12-Psa.22.18">Psa 22:12-18</reference>, prays with the confidence of being heard and delivered, <reference osisRef="Psa.22.19-Psa.22.24">Psa 22:19-24</reference>; praises God. and foretells the conversion of the nations to the true religion, <reference osisRef="Psa.22.25-Psa.22.31">Psa 22:25-31</reference>. <div eID="gen19186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19187" type="x-p"/> The title of this Psalm, To the chief Musician upon Aijeleth Shahar, A Psalm of David, has given rise to many conjectures. The words אילת השחר aiyeleth hashshachar are translated in the margin, "the hind of the morning;" but what was this? Was it the name of a musical instrument? or of a tune? or of a band of music? Calmet argues for the last, and translates "A Psalm of David, addressed to the Musicmaster who presides over the Band called the Morning Hind." This is more likely than any of the other conjectures I have seen. But aiyeleth hashshachar may be the name of the Psalm itself, for it was customary among the Asiatics to give names to their poetic compositions which often bore no relation to the subject itself. Mr. Harmer and others have collected a few instances from D'Herbelot's Bibliotheque Orientale. I could add many more from MSS. in my own collection: - thus Saady calls a famous miscellaneous work of his Gulisstan, "The Country of Roses," or, "Tbe Rose Garden:" and yet there is nothing relative to such a country, nor concerning roses nor rose gardens, in the book. Another is called Negeristan, "The Gallery of Pietures;" yet no picture gallery is mentioned. Another Beharistan, "The Spring Season;" Bostan, "The Garden;" Anvar Soheely, "The Light of Canopus;" Bahar Danush, "The Garden of Knowledge;" Tuhfit Almumeneen, "The Gift of the Faithful," a treatise on medicine; Kemeea lsadut, "The Alchymy of Life;" Mukhzeen al Asrar, "The Magazine of Secrets;" Sulselet al Zahab, "The Golden Chain;" Zuhfit al Abrar, "The Rosary of the Pious:" Merat al Asrar, "The Mirror of Secrets;" Durj al Durar, "The most precious Jewels" Deru Majlis, "The Jewel of the Assembly;" Al Bordah, "The Variegated Garment;" a poem written by Al Basiree, in praise of the Mohammedan religion, in gratitude for a cure which he believed he received from the prophet who appeared to him in a dream. The poem is written in one hundred and sixty-two couplets, each of which ends with mim, the first letter in the name of Mohammed. <div eID="gen19187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19188" type="x-p"/> Scarcely one of the above titles, and their number might be easily trebled, bears any relation to the subject of the work to which it is prefixed, no more than Aijeleth Shahar bears to the matter contained in the twenty-second Psalm. Such titles are of very little importance in themselves; and of no farther use to us than as they serve to distinguish the different books, poems, or Psalms, to which they are prefixed. To me, many seem to have spent their time uselessly in the investigation of such subjects. See my note on <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.18">2Sam 1:18</reference> (note). <div eID="gen19188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19189" type="x-p"/> On the subject of the Psalm itself, there is considerable diversity of opinion: <div eID="gen19189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19190" type="x-p"/> 1. Some referring it all to David; <div eID="gen19190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19191" type="x-p"/> 2. Others referring it all to Christ; and, <div eID="gen19191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19192" type="x-p"/> 3. Some, because of the application of several verses of it to our Lord in his sufferings, take a middle way, and apply it primarily to David, and in a secondary or accommodated sense, to Christ. <div eID="gen19192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19193" type="x-p"/> Of this opinion was Theodore of Mopsuestia. who gave a very rational account of his own plan of interpretation; for which he was condemned by the second council of Constantinople or fifth Ecumenic council. Grotius and others have nearly copied his plan; and I think, with a little correction, it is the only safe one. That several parts of it relate to David, primarily, there is very little reason to doubt; that several passages may be applied by way of accommodation to our Lord, though originally belonging to and expressing the state of David, may be piously believed; and that it contains portions which are direct prophecies of our Lord's passion, death, and victory, appears too evident to be safely denied. On this plan I propose to treat it in the following paraphrase; keeping it as near to the Gospel standard as I can. Dr. Delaney supposes the Psalm to have been written by David when he was at Mahaniam, the very place where God appeared to Jacob in his distress. See Genesis 22: And on this supposition the third, fourth, and fifth verses may be easily and strikingly illustrated: Our fathers trusted in thee; why may not I? Thou didst deliver Them; why may not I expect deliverance also? They cried unto thee, trusted in thee, and were not confounded; I cry until thee, trust in thee; and why should I be confounded? For thou art the same God, thou changest not; and with thee there is no respect of persons. Thus David encouraged himself in the Lord; and these considerations helped to sustain him in his painful exercises and heavy distresses. <div eID="gen19193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19194" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19195" type="x-p"/> My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? - Show me the cause why thou hast abandoned me to my enemies; and why thou seemest to disregard my prayers and cries? For a full illustration of this passage, I beg the reader to refer to my note on <reference osisRef="Mat.27.46">Mat 27:46</reference>. <div eID="gen19195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19196" type="x-p"/> The words of my roaring? - שאגתי shaagathi, The Vulgate, Septuagint, Syriac, Ethiopic, and Arabic, with the Anglo-Saxon, make use of terms which may be thus translated: "My sins (or foolishness) are the cause why deliverance is so far from me." It appears that these versions have read שגגתי shegagathi, "my sin of ignorance," instead of שאגתי shaagathi, "my roaring:" but no MS. extant supports this reading.
entries.9d9ae31e00b278141b177288a54f41e3fc117266: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen19196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19197" type="x-p"/> I cry in the day-time, and in the night-season - This seems to be David's own experience; and the words seem to refer to his own case alone. Though I am not heard, and thou appearest to forget or abandon me; yet I continue to cry both day and night after thy salvation.
entries.39c596ed96a01fefcd70c9c63e8cb9ee7619dccd: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen19197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19198" type="x-p"/> But thou art holy - Though I be not heard, even while I cry earnestly, yet I cannot impute any fault or unkindness to my Maker; for thou art holy. and canst do nothing but what is right. This is the language of profound resignation, in trials the most difficult to be borne. <div eID="gen19198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19199" type="x-p"/> Inhabitest the praises of Israel - Thou dwellest in the sanctuary where the praises, thanksgivings, and sacrifices of thy people are continually offered.
entries.fe870fd7394335139ab7980ad4ae9fde4517dcda: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen19199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19200" type="x-p"/> Our fathers trusted in thee - David is supposed to have been, at the time of composing this Psalm, at Mahanaim, where Jacob was once in such great distress; where he wrestled with the angel, and was so signally blessed. David might well allude to this circumstance in order to strengthen his faith in God. I am now in the place where God so signally blessed the head and father of our tribes. I wrestle with God, as he did; may I not expect similar success?
entries.ee625c134730dc445afc191c90291549553893f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19201" type="x-p"/> They cried unto thee - So do I: They were delivered; so may I: They trusted in thee; I also trust in thee. And were not confounded; and is it likely that I shall be put to confusion?
entries.377c46553e4e6250f4d09b7ac8bf94a10a99160c: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen19201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19202" type="x-p"/> But I am a worm, and no man - I can see no sense in which our Lord could use these terms. David might well use them to express his vileness and worthlessness. The old Psalter gives this a remarkable turn: I am a worme, that es, I am borne of the mayden with outen manseede; and nout man anely, bot god als so: and nevir the latter, I am reprove of men. In spitting, buffetyng, and punging with the thornes and outkasting of folk; for thai chesed Barraban the thefe, and nought me.
entries.0ec3c6505b46836028a9be0da32494a232ab64bc: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen19202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19203" type="x-p"/> Laugh me to scorn - They utterly despised me; set me at naught; treated me with the utmost contempt. Laugh to scorn is so completely antiquated that it should be no longer used; derided, despised, treated with contempt, are much more expressive and are still in common use. <div eID="gen19203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19204" type="x-p"/> They shoot out the lip, they shake the head - This is applied by St. Matthew, to the conduct of the Jews towards our Lord, when he hung upon the cross; as is also the following verse. But both are primarily true of the insults which David suffered from Shimei and others during the rebellion of Absalom; and, as the cases were so similar, the evangelist thought proper to express a similar conduct to Jesus Christ by the same expressions. These insults our Lord literally received, no doubt David received the same.
entries.e3d8ffb09ab97f3a7e413b76cf70c41266f91bc7: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen19204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19205" type="x-p"/> But thou art he that took me out of the womb - Thou hast made me; and hast guided and defended me from my earliest infancy.
entries.a2b17bf43c9c5f62b0ab20967b3f63300c328c18: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen19205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19206" type="x-p"/> Be not far from me; for trouble is near - A present God is a present blessing. We always need the Divine help; but more especially when troubles and trials are at hand.
entries.d13a066b0c49b32f639cd5e258e399e6bbd60f11: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen19206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19207" type="x-p"/> Many bulls have compassed me - The bull is the emblem of brutal strength, that gores and tramples down all before it. Such was Absalom, Ahithophel, and others, who rose up in rebellion against David; and such were the Jewish rulers who conspired against Christ. <div eID="gen19207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19208" type="x-p"/> Strong bulls of Bashan - Bashan was a district beyond Jordan, very fertile, where they were accustomed to fatten cattle, which became, in consequence of the excellent pasture, the largest, as well as the fattest, in the country. See Calmet. All in whose hands were the chief power and influence became David's enemies; for Absalom had stolen away the hearts of all Israel. Against Christ, the chiefs both of Jews and Gentiles were united.
entries.f5ca046a3005ff42fe66e6e260b8b4384d6b719d: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen19208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19209" type="x-p"/> They gaped upon me - They were fiercely and madly beat on my destruction.
entries.4c7259d7978d37eadd2dfe79bacf0a2dbb704bcb: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen19209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19210" type="x-p"/> I am poured out like water - That is, as the old Psalter: Thai rought na mare to sla me than to spil water. <div eID="gen19210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19211" type="x-p"/> The images in this verse are strongly descriptivr of a person in the deepest distress; whose strength, courage, hope, and expectation of succor and relief, had entirely failed. <div eID="gen19211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19212" type="x-p"/> Our Lord's sufferings were extreme; but I cannot think there is any sound theologic sense in which these things can be spoken of Christ, either in his agony in the garden, or his death upon the cross.
entries.32bff82aa642db85d359cc26464c07fd7b200e08: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen19212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19213" type="x-p"/> My strength is dried up - All these expressions mark a most distressed and hopeless case. <div eID="gen19213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19214" type="x-p"/> Into the dust of death - This means only that he was apparently brought nigh to the grave, and consequent corruption, this latter David saw; but Jesus Christ never saw corruption.
entries.69d3955cb05481a551011c6891da61d884c69214: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen19214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19215" type="x-p"/> For dogs have compassed me - This may refer to the Gentiles, the Roman soldiers, and others by whom our Lord was surrounded in his trial, and at his cross. <div eID="gen19215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19216" type="x-p"/> They pierced my hands and my feet - The other sufferings David, as a type of our Lord, might pass through; but the piercing of the hands and feet was peculiar to our Lord; therefore, this verse may pass for a direct revelavion. Our Lord's hands and feet were pierced when he was nailed to the cross, David's never were pierced. <div eID="gen19216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19217" type="x-p"/> But there is a various reading here which is of great importance. Instead of כארו caaru, they pierced, which is what is called the kethib, or marginal reading, and which our translators have followed; the keri or textual reading is כארי caari, as a lion. In support of each reading there are both MSS. and eminent critics. The Chaldee has, "Biting as a lion my hands and my feet;" but the Syriac, Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic read, "they pierced or digged;" and in the Anglo-Saxon the words translate: "They dalve (digged) hands mine, and feet mine." <div eID="gen19217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19218" type="x-p"/> The Complutensian Polyglot has כארו caaru, they digged or pierced, in the text; for which it gives כרה carah, to cut, dig, or penetrate, in the margin, as the root whence כארו is derived.
